questions.q: If the derivative of the function $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}b x^2+a x+4 ; & x \geq-1 \\ a x^2+b ; & x < -1\end{array}\right.$ is everywhere continuous, then
questions.solution:
The function $f(x)$ is defined as $f(x) = bx^2 + ax + 4$ for $x \geq -1$ and $f(x) = ax^2 + b$ for $x < -1$.

For the derivative $f'(x)$ to be continuous everywhere, $f(x)$ must be continuous at $x = -1$. Thus, $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f(x) = f(-1)$.

Calculating the limits: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (ax^2 + b) = a + b$ and $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (bx^2 + ax + 4) = b - a + 4$.

Equating these, $a + b = b - a + 4$, which simplifies to $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

Now, consider the derivative $f'(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{cc} 2bx + a; & x > -1 \\ 2ax; & x < -1 \end{array}\right\}$.

For $f'(x)$ to be continuous at $x = -1$, the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative must be equal: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f'(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f'(x)$.

Substituting $a = 2$: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (2ax) = 2(2)(-1) = -4$.

The right-hand derivative is $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (2bx + a) = 2b(-1) + 2 = -2b + 2$.

Equating these, $-4 = -2b + 2$, which gives $2b = 6$, so $b = 3$.

Thus, $a = 2$ and $b = 3$.

Answer: $a=2, b=3$

options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.

$\begin{aligned} \text{ Consider } \frac{x}{[x]} \leq f(x) \leq \sqrt{6-x}\\
& \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \frac{x}{[x]}=\frac{2}{1}=2
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \sqrt{6-x}=2 \\ \text{$ and $} \therefore \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)=2
\end{aligned} [By Sandwich theorem]
Now \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \frac{x}{[x]}=1, \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \sqrt{6-x}=2$
Hence by Sandwich theorem $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} f(x)$ does not exists.
